rules.title: The verb be in the present
rules.description:
**The idea** — English needs a verb in every sentence, even when you only say who someone is, where something is or what it is like. The verb `be` links the subject to a name, a job, an age, a place or a quality. It changes its form for each person.

**The form**
- Positive: `I am`, `you are`, `he is`, `she is`, `it is`, `we are`, `you are`, `they are`
- Contracted: `I'm`, `you're`, `he's`, `she's`, `it's`, `we're`, `they're`
- Negative: add `not` after the verb: `am not`, `is not` (`isn't`), `are not` (`aren't`); there is no `amn't`
- Question: the verb goes before the subject: `Are you`, `Is she`, `Am I`
- Short answers repeat the verb: `Yes, I am`, `No, he isn't`; a positive short answer is never contracted

**When it applies**
- Names, jobs, nationalities and descriptions: signal words `my name`, `a teacher`, `from`, `tall`
- Age, feelings and states: `ten years old`, `hungry`, `cold`, `afraid`
- Places and time: `at home`, `in the kitchen`, `here`, `late`

**When it does NOT apply** — With ordinary actions use the present simple (`work`, `live`), not `be`. Test: if the word after the subject is an action, use no `be`; if it is a name, place, age or quality, use `be`.

**Typical mistakes**
- Leaving out `be`: learners copy the pattern of a bare noun or adjective, but English always needs the verb
- Using `have` for age, hunger or cold, because it seems to mean 'own'; English uses `be` for these
- Using one form for all persons (`I is`, `they is`): learn `am`, `is`, `are` as one set

**Register and usage** — Contractions are normal in speech and informal writing; full forms are used for emphasis and in formal writing.
rules.llmDescription: Present forms am, is, are: missing be before a noun, adjective or place; wrong person such as 'I is' or 'they is'; 'have' instead of be for age or feelings.

rules.title: Subject pronouns
rules.description:
**The idea** — A pronoun replaces a noun so that you do not repeat it. English sentences nearly always need an explicit subject, so a pronoun must stand before the verb, even for weather and time. The subject form is different from the object form.

**The form**
- Subject pronouns: `I`, `you`, `he`, `she`, `it`, `we`, `you`, `they`
- Object forms (never used as subject): `me`, `him`, `her`, `us`, `them`
- `he` is for a man or boy, `she` for a woman or girl, `it` for things, animals and ideas
- `they` is the plural for people and things
- Empty subject `it` stands before the verb in weather, time and distance: `it is raining`, `it is late`

**When it applies**
- Before every finite verb that has no other subject: signal words are a verb with no noun before it
- Instead of a name already mentioned: `Anna` becomes `she`, `the books` becomes `they`
- In answers and short sentences: `I am`, `we work`, `they live`

**When it does NOT apply** — After a verb or preposition use the object forms (`me`, `him`, `them`), not the subject forms. Test: if the pronoun does the action, use the subject form; if it receives the action, use the object form.

**Typical mistakes**
- Dropping the subject (`am tired`, `is cold`), because the verb ending shows the person in other languages; English needs the pronoun
- Using `me`, `him` or `them` as subject because they sound like the usual form after verbs
- Using `it` for a person or `he/she` for a thing; choose by the noun being replaced

**Register and usage** — Subject pronouns are required in all registers; only very informal notes may drop them.

rules.title: Using a and an
rules.description:
**The idea** — English marks a single, non-specific countable thing with a small word before the noun. This word is `a` or `an`, and the choice depends only on the first sound of the next word, not on its spelling.

**The form**
- `a` before a consonant sound: `a book`, `a teacher`, `a big house`
- `an` before a vowel sound: `an apple`, `an engineer`, `an old house`
- The sound decides, not the letter: `a university`, `a European`, `an hour`, `an honest man`
- The word that counts is the one directly after the article, often an adjective
- No plural form: for plurals use no article or `some`; negative and question forms use the same article

**When it applies**
- A singular countable noun mentioned for the first time: signal words `there is`, `I have`, `she has`
- Jobs, types and descriptions: `he is a nurse`, `it is an easy test`
- Quantities in phrases: `a lot`, `once a week`, `twice a day`

**When it does NOT apply** — Before plural and uncountable nouns use no article (`books`, `water`, `advice`). Test: if you can say `one` before the noun, use `a/an`; if you cannot (`one water`), use no article.

**Typical mistakes**
- Choosing by the letter, not the sound (`an university`, `a hour`); say the word aloud and listen
- Forgetting the article with a singular noun, because the noun alone sounds complete
- Using `a` with plural or uncountable nouns (`a students`, `a water`); `a` means `one`

**Register and usage** — The rule is the same in speech and writing; in fast speech `an` often sounds linked to the next word.

**Exceptions and anything worth knowing**
- Abbreviations follow the sound of the first letter: `an MBA`, `a UN report`
rules.llmDescription: Indefinite article a and an: wrong choice before vowel or consonant sounds (an university, a hour), missing article before a singular countable noun, a before plural or uncountable nouns.

rules.title: Regular plural nouns
rules.description:
**The idea** — English marks more than one thing by changing the end of the noun. Most nouns follow one simple pattern, and a few spelling changes keep the word easy to say.

**The form**
- Most nouns add `-s`: `book` becomes `books`, `car` becomes `cars`
- After `-s`, `-x`, `-z`, `-ch`, `-sh` add `-es`: `bus` becomes `buses`, `box` becomes `boxes`, `watch` becomes `watches`, `dish` becomes `dishes`
- Consonant plus `-y`: change `y` to `-ies`: `city` becomes `cities`, `baby` becomes `babies`
- Vowel plus `-y`: just add `-s`: `boy` becomes `boys`, `day` becomes `days`
- Some nouns in `-o` add `-es` (`tomato`, `potato`, `hero`); most others add `-s` (`photo`, `piano`)
- Nouns in `-f` or `-fe` often change to `-ves`: `leaf` becomes `leaves`, `knife` becomes `knives`

**When it applies**
- After numbers above one: signal words `two`, `three`, `many`, `several`
- After `these`, `those`, `a few`, `both`
- With plural verbs: the verb agrees, such as `are`, `have`

**When it does NOT apply** — Irregular plurals (`child`, `man`, `foot`) and uncountable nouns (`water`, `money`) do not follow this pattern. Test: if the noun can be counted and has no special form, add `-s` or `-es`.

**Typical mistakes**
- Adding only `-s` to words in `-x`, `-ch`, `-sh`, `-s` (`boxs`); the plural must be pronounceable
- Writing `-ys` after a consonant (`babys`) or `-ies` after a vowel (`boies`)
- Leaving the noun singular after a number or `many`

**Register and usage** — Spelling rules are the same in all registers.

rules.title: Third person singular -s
rules.description:
**The idea** — The present simple tells about habits, facts and routines. In this tense the verb is the same for most persons, but it takes a special ending when the subject is one other person or thing: he, she, it.

**The form**
- `I`, `you`, `we`, `they`: base verb: `work`, `live`, `play`
- `he`, `she`, `it` and any singular noun: base verb plus `-s`: `works`, `lives`, `plays`
- After `-s`, `-x`, `-z`, `-ch`, `-sh`, `-o` add `-es`: `watches`, `goes`, `fixes`
- Consonant plus `-y`: `-ies`: `study` becomes `studies`, `cry` becomes `cries`
- `have` becomes `has`; `be` has its own forms (`is`)
- In negatives and questions the `-s` moves to `does`, and the verb returns to the base form

**When it applies**
- Habits and routines with `he`, `she`, `it`: signal words `every day`, `always`, `usually`, `on Mondays`
- General facts about one person or thing: `the sun rises`, `water boils`
- Singular names and nouns as subject: `my mother`, `the shop`, `Tom`

**When it does NOT apply** — With `I`, `you`, `we`, `they` and plural nouns the verb takes no `-s`. Test: if you can replace the subject with `he`, `she` or `it`, add `-s`; if you can replace it with `they`, add nothing.

**Typical mistakes**
- Forgetting the `-s` because the meaning is clear without it; the ending carries the agreement
- Adding `-s` to every verb, even after `I` or `they`, after learning the ending once
- Writing `-s` instead of `-es` (`watchs`, `gos`) or `have` instead of `has`

**Register and usage** — The ending is required in all registers; omitting it marks a speaker as a learner.

rules.title: Negatives with do not
rules.description:
**The idea** — To say that a habit or fact is not true, English does not put `not` after the main verb. It uses a helper verb, `do`, to carry the negative and the person, and the main verb stays in its simple form.

**The form**
- `I`, `you`, `we`, `they`: `do not` + base verb
- `he`, `she`, `it`: `does not` + base verb
- Contracted: `don't`, `doesn't`
- The main verb is always the base form, with no `-s`: the `-s` is already in `does`
- Question form: `Do you ...?`, `Does she ...?`
- Short answers: `Yes, I do` / `No, she doesn't`

**When it applies**
- Negative habits and routines: signal words `never`, `not often`, `on Sundays`
- Negative facts and tastes: `like`, `want`, `know`, `need`
- Any ordinary verb except `be` and modal verbs

**When it does NOT apply** — The verb `be` and modals (`can`) make negatives by adding `not` directly: `is not`, `cannot`. Test: if the verb is `be` or a modal, add `not`; if it is any other verb, use `do/does not`.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using `no` before the verb, because `no` is the usual negative word in other contexts; use `not` with a helper
- Keeping the `-s` on the verb after `doesn't`, because the ending feels necessary
- Using `don't` with `he/she/it`, or `don't` with `be`
- Using a double negative with `no` or `nothing`; English wants `any` in a negative sentence

**Register and usage** — Contractions are standard in speech; `do not` is used for emphasis or in formal writing.

rules.title: Questions with do and does
rules.description:
**The idea** — A question about a habit or fact needs a helper verb. The helper `do` or `does` stands first and signals the question, and the main verb stays in its simple form.

**The form**
- Yes/no question: `Do` + `I/you/we/they` + base verb: `Do you like ...?`
- With `he/she/it` and singular nouns: `Does` + subject + base verb
- The main verb has no `-s`: the `-s` lives in `does`
- Question word first: `Where do you ...`, `What does he ...`, `Why do they ...`
- Short answers: `Yes, I do`, `No, she doesn't`; the main verb is not repeated
- With `be` and modals there is no `do`: `Are you ...`, `Can you ...`

**When it applies**
- Questions about routines and habits: signal words `every day`, `usually`, `often`
- Questions about likes, facts and places: `like`, `live`, `work`, `speak`
- Questions with `who`, `what`, `where`, `when`, `why`, `how` plus another verb

**When it does NOT apply** — If the question word is the subject (`Who lives here`), there is no `do`. Test: if the question word replaces the subject, no helper; if it asks about something else, add `do/does`.

**Typical mistakes**
- Leaving out `do` or `does` and only raising the voice, which works in other situations but not in a full question
- Using `do` with he/she/it, or `does` with they or a plural noun
- Keeping `-s` on the main verb after `does`
- Using `be` as a helper in the present simple (`Are you work`)

**Register and usage** — Spoken questions can be short (`Like it?`), but in learner English always use the full form.

rules.title: There is and there are
rules.description:
**The idea** — To say that something exists or is present in a place, English starts with the empty word `there` and then the verb `be`. The real subject comes after the verb, and the verb agrees with it.

**The form**
- Singular and uncountable: `there is` + `a/an` noun or `some/any` + uncountable: `there is a bank`, `there is some milk`
- Plural: `there are` + plural noun: `there are two chairs`
- Contracted: `there's` (not `there're` in writing)
- Negative: `there isn't`, `there aren't`; with `any` for plural and uncountable
- Question: `Is there ...?`, `Are there ...?`; answers: `Yes, there is` / `No, there aren't`
- Place words usually come at the end: `in the room`, `near the station`

**When it applies**
- Saying what a place contains: signal words `in the room`, `in my town`, `on the table`
- Introducing a new thing for the first time: `there is a ...`
- Asking if something exists or is available: `is there ...`, `are there any ...`

**When it does NOT apply** — To say what a known thing is, use `it is`; to say what someone owns, use `have`. Test: if the thing is new and you only say it exists here, use `there is/are`; if you describe a known thing, use `it is`.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using the wrong verb form for the number of the noun that follows (`there is three books`), because `there` seems to be the subject
- Using `have` for existence (`In my room have a bed`), a pattern copied from other verbs
- Using `it is` to introduce a new thing instead of `there is`
- Using `there` with `be` in the wrong word order in questions

**Register and usage** — `there's` is common even before plurals in fast speech, but in writing keep `there are` for plurals.
rules.llmDescription: Existential there is and there are: verb not agreeing with the noun after it, have or it is used instead of there is, wrong order in questions and negatives with there.

rules.title: Can for ability
rules.description:
**The idea** — To say what someone is able to do, English uses a small helper verb, `can`. It is a modal verb: it never changes for the person and it is followed directly by the base form of the next verb.

**The form**
- Positive: subject + `can` + base verb: no `-s`, no `to`
- Negative: `cannot` (one word) or `can't`; `can not` is rare and emphatic
- Question: `can` goes before the subject: `Can you ...?`, `Can she ...?`
- Short answers: `Yes, I can` / `No, he can't`
- No `do` or `does`: `can` makes its own questions and negatives
- Same form for all persons: `I can`, `he can`, `they can`

**When it applies**
- Skills: signal words `swim`, `speak`, `play`, `drive`, `cook`
- Present possibility or permission in simple requests: `can I sit here`, `can you help me`
- Senses with verbs of perceiving: `I can see`, `I can hear`

**When it does NOT apply** — For ability in the past use `could` or `was able to`; for obligation use `must` or `have to`. Test: if you mean 'I am able to now' use `can`; if the ability was in the past, change to `could`.

**Typical mistakes**
- Adding `to` after `can` (`can to swim`), because many verbs take `to`; modals never do
- Adding `-s` to `can` or to the next verb after `he/she/it`, because the third person usually has `-s`
- Using `do` with `can` (`do you can`), a pattern copied from ordinary verbs
- Putting a verb in the `-ing` form after `can`

**Register and usage** — `can't` is normal in speech; `cannot` is common in written rules; `can` for permission is informal, `may` is formal.

rules.title: Past simple regular verbs
rules.description:
**The idea** — To tell about a finished action in the past, English changes the verb itself. Regular verbs all use the same ending, and the form is the same for every person.

**The form**
- Most verbs add `-ed`: `work` becomes `worked`, `watch` becomes `watched`
- Verbs ending in `-e` add only `-d`: `live` becomes `lived`, `arrive` becomes `arrived`
- Consonant plus `-y` becomes `-ied`: `study` becomes `studied`, `try` becomes `tried`; vowel plus `-y` adds `-ed`: `play` becomes `played`
- One-syllable verbs with a short vowel and one final consonant double it: `stop` becomes `stopped`, `plan` becomes `planned`
- The same form for `I`, `you`, `he`, `we`, `they`: no `-s`
- Negatives and questions use `did` (see the rule on `did`)

**When it applies**
- Finished events with a past time: signal words `yesterday`, `last week`, `two years ago`, `in 2015`
- Series of past actions in a story: `opened`, `looked`, `walked`
- Past states that are over: `lived`, `wanted`

**When it does NOT apply** — Irregular verbs have their own forms (`go` becomes `went`), and the present perfect is used when the time is not finished or not named. Test: if you can name a finished time, use the past simple; if the verb is irregular, use its special form.

**Typical mistakes**
- Leaving the verb in the base form after a past time word, because the time word already shows the past
- Spelling errors: `studyed`, `stoped`, `plaied`; apply the spelling pattern carefully
- Changing only the first verb in a list and leaving the other verbs in the present

**Register and usage** — The ending is pronounced three ways (`/t/`, `/d/`, `/ɪd/`), but the spelling is always `-ed`.

rules.title: Irregular past simple forms
rules.description:
**The idea** — Many of the most common English verbs do not take `-ed` in the past. They have their own past forms, which come from older patterns of the language, and you must learn them one by one.

**The form**
- The past simple is one form for all persons: `went`, `saw`, `had`, `made`
- Frequent groups: vowel change (`sing` becomes `sang`, `drive` becomes `drove`), `-ought/-aught` (`buy` becomes `bought`, `teach` becomes `taught`), unchanged (`put`, `cut`, `read`)
- Core verbs: `be` becomes `was/were`, `go` becomes `went`, `have` becomes `had`, `do` becomes `did`
- Others: `eat` becomes `ate`, `take` becomes `took`, `come` becomes `came`, `write` becomes `wrote`, `think` becomes `thought`
- Negative and questions use `did` + base verb, never the past form

**When it applies**
- Finished events with past time words: `yesterday`, `last night`, `in 2010`, `ago`
- Telling stories in order: first, then, after that
- Past habits and states that are over

**When it does NOT apply** — After `did`, `to` or a modal the verb is in the base form, and with `have` the past participle is used. Test: if there is `did` or `have` before the verb, do not use the simple past form.

**Typical mistakes**
- Adding `-ed` to an irregular verb (`goed`, `buyed`, `eated`), because the regular pattern is overgeneralised
- Using the base form after a past time word
- Mixing up the past simple and the participle (`I seen`, `he did went`)

**Register and usage** — Irregular verbs are the most frequent verbs in speech, so use them correctly early.

rules.title: Did in past questions and negatives
rules.description:
**The idea** — In the past simple, the past marker moves to a helper verb, `did`, when you ask a question or deny something. After `did` the main verb returns to its simple base form, because the past is already shown once.

**The form**
- Negative: subject + `did not` (`didn't`) + base verb
- Yes/no question: `Did` + subject + base verb
- Question word: `Where did you ...`, `What did she ...`, `Why did they ...`
- Short answers: `Yes, I did` / `No, he didn't`
- The same `did` for every person and number: there is no `-s` or `-ed` on the main verb
- With `be` there is no `did`: `was not`, `Were you`

**When it applies**
- Questions about finished events: signal words `yesterday`, `last week`, `ago`, `when`
- Negative statements about the past: `didn't go`, `didn't see`
- Both regular and irregular verbs

**When it does NOT apply** — With `be`, with modals and when the question word is the subject (`Who called`), there is no `did`. Test: if the main verb is an ordinary verb in a past question or negative, use `did`.

**Typical mistakes**
- Keeping the past form after `did` (`did you went`, `didn't liked`), because the past seems to need marking on the verb
- Using `do` in a past question because the time word is forgotten
- Leaving out `did` and using only `no` or word order
- Putting `did` after the subject instead of before it in a question

**Register and usage** — `didn't` is normal in speech and in most writing.

rules.title: The present continuous
rules.description:
**The idea** — To show that something is happening now, around now, or is a temporary situation, English uses the verb `be` plus the `-ing` form. The speaker looks at the action while it is in progress, not as a habit.

**The form**
- Positive: `am/is/are` + verb + `-ing`: `I am working`, `she is working`, `they are working`
- Negative: `am/is/are` + `not` + verb + `-ing`; contracted `isn't`, `aren't`
- Question: `am/is/are` + subject + verb + `-ing`: `Are you working?`
- Spelling of `-ing`: drop a final silent `-e` (`make`, `making`); double the consonant after a short vowel (`run`, `running`, `sit`, `sitting`); `-ie` becomes `-ying` (`lie`, `lying`)
- `be` changes with the person; the `-ing` form never changes
- No `do` or `does` in this tense

**When it applies**
- Actions in progress at the moment of speaking: signal words `now`, `at the moment`, `look!`, `listen!`
- Temporary situations: `this week`, `these days`, `today`
- Changing situations: `getting`, `becoming`

**When it does NOT apply** — For habits and permanent facts use the present simple; state verbs (`know`, `like`, `want`) rarely take `-ing`. Test: if it happens regularly or is always true, use the present simple; if it is happening now or only for a time, use the continuous.

**Typical mistakes**
- Leaving out `be` (`they playing`), because the `-ing` form seems enough
- Leaving out `-ing` after `be` (`I am work`), or putting `do` before it
- Wrong spelling: `runing`, `makeing`

**Register and usage** — Contractions (`I'm`, `she's`) are the norm in speech.

rules.title: Going to for plans
rules.description:
**The idea** — To talk about plans made before now, or about something you can see is about to happen, English uses `be going to`. The speaker has a decision or evidence in the present, so the future is already on its way.

**The form**
- Positive: `am/is/are` + `going to` + base verb
- Negative: `am/is/are` + `not` + `going to` + base verb
- Question: `Am/Is/Are` + subject + `going to` + base verb
- Contracted: `I'm going to`, `she isn't going to`
- The verb after `to` is always the base form, with no `-s` and no `-ing`
- Fast speech: `gonna`; informal and not written in careful text

**When it applies**
- Plans and intentions: signal words `tomorrow`, `next week`, `this weekend`, `soon`
- Predictions from evidence in the present: `look at the clouds`, `be careful`
- Questions about someone's plans: `what are you going to do`

**When it does NOT apply** — For sudden decisions at the moment of speaking, and for neutral predictions, use `will`. Test: if you decided before speaking or you can see the sign now, use `going to`; if you decide now, use `will`.

**Typical mistakes**
- Leaving out `be` (`I going to buy`), because `going to` feels like one block
- Putting a second verb in the past or `-ing` after `to` (`going to bought`)
- Using `go` instead of `going` (`are go to travel`)
- Wrong question order: `What you are going to do`

**Register and usage** — `going to` is the normal spoken future for plans; `gonna` is for relaxed speech.

rules.title: Will for decisions and predictions
rules.description:
**The idea** — `Will` is the English tool for the future that comes from the speaker's view at the moment of speaking: a decision made now, an offer, a promise or an opinion about what will happen. It is a modal verb, so it stays the same for every person.

**The form**
- Positive: subject + `will` + base verb; contracted `I'll`, `she'll`, `they'll`
- Negative: `will not` or `won't` + base verb
- Question: `Will` + subject + base verb; question word first: `When will you ...`
- No `to` after `will`, no `-s`, no `-ing`: `will` is followed by the bare verb
- No `do` or `does` with `will`
- Short answers: `Yes, I will` / `No, she won't`

**When it applies**
- Sudden decisions and offers: `I'll help you`, `I'll answer`
- Promises and warnings: `I will call you`, `you'll be late`
- Predictions and opinions: signal words `I think`, `probably`, `maybe`, `tomorrow`

**When it does NOT apply** — For plans made earlier or things you can see happening, use `be going to`. Test: if you decide right now or give an opinion, use `will`; if the plan already exists, use `going to`.

**Typical mistakes**
- Adding `to` after `will` (`will to go`), because other verbs take `to`
- Adding `-s` or `-ing` to the main verb (`will goes`, `will raining`)
- Using `do` with `will`, or putting `not` in the wrong place (`will be not`)
- Using the present simple for a decision made now

**Register and usage** — `shall` is used in formal British offers; `will` is the neutral choice.

rules.title: Comparative adjectives
rules.description:
**The idea** — To say that one thing has more of a quality than another, English changes the adjective or puts a small word before it. The choice depends on how long the adjective is, and the second item is introduced by `than`.

**The form**
- Short adjectives (one syllable): add `-er`: `tall` becomes `taller`, `cheap` becomes `cheaper`
- Ending in `-e`: add `-r`: `nice` becomes `nicer`
- One vowel plus one consonant: double the consonant: `big` becomes `bigger`, `hot` becomes `hotter`
- Consonant plus `-y`: `-ier`: `happy` becomes `happier`, `easy` becomes `easier`
- Long adjectives (two or more syllables): `more` + adjective: `more interesting`, `more expensive`
- Irregular: `good` becomes `better`, `bad` becomes `worse`, `far` becomes `farther/further`
- Link with `than`: `than me`, `than yesterday`

**When it applies**
- Comparing two things or people: signal words `than`, `a bit`, `much`, `a lot`
- Comparing the same thing at two times: `today`, `last year`

**When it does NOT apply** — To say that something is the highest of three or more, use the superlative (`the tallest`); to say two things are equal, use `as ... as`. Test: if you compare two things with `than`, use the comparative.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using `more` before a short adjective (`more big`), because `more` works for long adjectives
- Using both `more` and `-er` (`more happier`)
- Writing `that` instead of `than`
- Adding `-er` to a long adjective (`interestinger`)
- Spelling: `easyer`, `bigest` for `bigger`

**Register and usage** — `further` is common for abstract distance, `farther` for physical distance.

rules.title: The definite article the
rules.description:
**The idea** — `The` points to a thing that speaker and listener can both identify: it was mentioned before, it is unique, or the situation makes clear which one. It marks 'this one that we both know'.

**The form**
- `the` is one form for singular and plural, countable and uncountable nouns
- Pronunciation: `/ðə/` before a consonant sound, `/ði/` before a vowel sound
- Before an adjective: `the old house`; superlative: `the best`, `the first`
- Fixed uses: `the sun`, `the moon`, `the sky`, `the world`, `the Earth`
- No `the` before general plurals and uncountables: `people`, `music`, `life`
- No `the` before sports, meals and most languages: `football`, `breakfast`, `English`

**When it applies**
- A noun already mentioned: signal words `a cat ... the cat`
- Unique things and roles: `the sun`, `the president`, `the manager`
- Things clear from context: `the door`, `the salt`, `the station`
- Superlatives, ordinals and `the same`: `the best`, `the first floor`

**When it does NOT apply** — For something new and non-specific use `a/an`; for general plurals and uncountables use no article. Test: if the listener knows exactly which one you mean, use `the`; if you speak about the idea in general, use none.

**Typical mistakes**
- Leaving out `the` before a known or unique noun, because the noun alone sounds enough
- Using `the` with generalisations (`the life`, `the money`, `the football`)
- Omitting `the` in superlatives and before ordinals

**Register and usage** — The rules are the same in speech and writing.

rules.title: Much, many and a lot of
rules.description:
**The idea** — English asks first: can you count the thing? Countable nouns (`book`, `friend`) have plurals and numbers. Uncountable nouns (`water`, `money`, `time`, `information`) do not. The word for 'a large amount' depends on this.

**The form**
- `many` + plural countable noun: `many books`, `many people`
- `much` + uncountable noun: `much time`, `much money`
- `a lot of` / `lots of` + either type, mainly in positive sentences
- `much` and `many` are normal in negatives and questions: `not much`, `how many`, `how much`
- In positive sentences `much` is rare in speech; use `a lot of`
- Uncountable nouns have no plural and no `a`: `information`, `advice`, `furniture`, `homework`, `news`

**When it applies**
- Questions about amount: signal words `how much`, `how many`
- Negatives: `not much`, `not many`, `too much`, `too many`
- Positive statements with a large amount: `a lot of`, `lots of`

**When it does NOT apply** — For a small amount use `a few` (countable) or `a little` (uncountable); for a positive large amount in speech use `a lot of`. Test: if you can add `-s` or put a number before it, use `many`; if not, use `much`.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using `much` with plural nouns, or `many` with uncountables (`many time`, `much books`)
- Using `much` in positive sentences, where it sounds formal or odd
- Giving uncountable nouns a plural (`informations`, `furnitures`, `advices`)
- Using `a` with an uncountable noun

**Register and usage** — `a lot of` is neutral and the best default in positive sentences.

rules.title: In, on and at for time
rules.description:
**The idea** — English uses three small words to place an event in time. They work like boxes of different sizes: `in` for long periods, `on` for days and dates, `at` for exact points.

**The form**
- `at` + clock time and points: `at 5 o'clock`, `at noon`, `at midnight`, `at night`, `at the weekend` (British)
- `on` + days and dates: `on Monday`, `on 5 May`, `on Christmas Day`, `on Friday morning`
- `in` + months, seasons, years, centuries: `in July`, `in winter`, `in 1998`, `in the 21st century`
- `in` + parts of the day: `in the morning`, `in the afternoon`, `in the evening`
- `in` + a period from now: `in two weeks`, `in an hour`
- No preposition before `next`, `last`, `this`, `every`, `today`, `tomorrow`, `yesterday`

**When it applies**
- Saying when something happens: signal words `when`, `what time`, `which day`
- Schedules, birthdays, appointments and habits

**When it does NOT apply** — For duration use `for` (`for two hours`), for a start point use `since`, and for an end point use `until` or `by`. Test: if you name a clock time use `at`; a day or date use `on`; a longer period use `in`.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using `at` for days or months, or `in` for clock time, because one word is chosen for all time phrases
- Using `on` before months and years
- Using `in` for `night` (`in night`) and `on` for `the morning`
- Adding a preposition before `next` or `last`

**Register and usage** — `at the weekend` is British; American English says `on the weekend`.

rules.title: Present perfect with for and since
rules.description:
**The idea** — When a situation began in the past and is still true now, English connects both times in one verb form, the present perfect. The speaker says: it started then and it continues until now. The words `for` and `since` measure this period.

**The form**
- `have/has` + past participle: `have lived`, `has worked`, `has been`
- Negative: `have not` (`haven't`) / `has not` (`hasn't`) + participle
- Question: `Have/Has` + subject + participle; `How long have you ...?`
- `for` + length of time: `for two years`, `for a long time`, `for ages`
- `since` + starting point: `since 2010`, `since Monday`, `since I was a child`
- Regular participles end in `-ed`; irregular ones must be learned: `known`, `been`, `had`

**When it applies**
- A state or action that began earlier and continues now: signal words `for`, `since`, `how long`
- With state verbs: `be`, `know`, `have`, `live`, `work`
- With `all day`, `all my life`, `recently` for unfinished periods

**When it does NOT apply** — If the situation is finished or the time is named as past (`in 2010`, `last year`), use the past simple. Test: if it still goes on now, use the present perfect with `for/since`; if it is over, use the past simple.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using the present simple (`I live here since 2018`), because the situation is true now; English needs the perfect
- Mixing up `for` and `since` (`since five years`, `for 2010`); `for` takes a length, `since` takes a starting point
- Using the past simple in `how long` questions about the present
- Using the base form or the past form instead of the participle

**Register and usage** — Contractions (`I've`, `she's`) are normal in speech and informal writing.

rules.title: Present perfect with ever and never
rules.description:
**The idea** — To talk about life experience without saying when it happened, English uses the present perfect. The exact time is not important; what matters is whether the experience exists in a person's life up to now.

**The form**
- `have/has` + past participle: `have been`, `has seen`, `have eaten`
- `ever` in questions: `Have you ever ...?` and after superlatives: `the best film I have ever seen`
- `never` in statements: `have never` + participle; it already means `not ever`
- Negative with `not`: `haven't` + participle (without `never`); never use `not` and `never` together
- Position: `ever` and `never` go between `have/has` and the participle
- `been` for visits that are finished (`have been to Rome`); `gone` means the person is still there

**When it applies**
- Asking about experience: signal words `ever`, `before`, `so far`, `in your life`
- Denying experience: `never`, `not yet`
- Superlatives of experience: `the most ... I have ever`

**When it does NOT apply** — With a specific past time (`last year`, `in 2015`, `yesterday`) use the past simple. Test: if you can add a finished time, use the past simple; if the time is open, use the present perfect.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using `ever` in positive statements (`I have ever been`), because `ever` seems to mean 'once'; use `never` or no adverb
- Using the past form or base form instead of the participle (`ever ate`, `ever play`)
- Double negatives: `haven't never`, `has never not`
- Putting `never` in front of `have`

**Register and usage** — `ever` is the natural word in questions and superlatives; `never` is common in speech.

rules.title: The first conditional
rules.description:
**The idea** — The first conditional speaks about a real, possible situation in the future and its likely result. The speaker thinks the condition may well happen, so the sentence has two parts: the `if` part and the result part.

**The form**
- `if` + present simple, `will` + base verb: the condition is in the present form, the result in the future form
- The result clause can come first, without a comma: result + `if` + present simple
- Negative: `if you don't ...`, `will not` / `won't`; `unless` + positive verb means `if not`
- Question: `What will you do if ...?`; the `if` part stays in the present simple
- Other results: `can`, `may`, `might` or an imperative instead of `will`
- Never put `will` right after `if` (`if it will rain`)

**When it applies**
- Real future possibilities: signal words `if`, `unless`, `as soon as`, `when`
- Warnings, promises and threats
- Plans that depend on something else, such as weather or time

**When it does NOT apply** — For an unlikely or imaginary situation use the second conditional (`if` + past); for a general truth use the present simple in both parts. Test: if the condition is realistic and about the future, use present + `will`; if it is imaginary, use past + `would`.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using `will` in the `if` clause, because the meaning is future; English uses the present simple there
- Using `would` or the present simple in the result, so the result loses its future meaning
- Using `unless` with a negative verb (a double negative)

**Register and usage** — Both orders are normal; put a comma after the `if` clause when it comes first.

rules.title: Must and have to
rules.description:
**The idea** — English has two ways to say that something is necessary. `Must` usually shows the speaker's own feeling or a strong rule, while `have to` shows an outside rule or a fact. Their negatives mean very different things.

**The form**
- `must` + base verb: one form for all persons; no `to`, no `-s`
- `have to` + base verb: `have to` with `I/you/we/they`, `has to` with `he/she/it`
- Negative of `have to`: `don't/doesn't have to` + base verb: not necessary
- Negative of `must`: `must not` / `mustn't` + base verb: forbidden
- Questions: `Do you have to ...?` for `have to`; `Must I ...?` is formal and rare
- Past: `must` has no past form, so use `had to` + base verb; questions and negatives use `did` + `have to`

**When it applies**
- Rules, laws and instructions: signal words `must not`, `you have to`, `it is necessary`
- Duties from work, school or other people
- The speaker's strong personal need: `I must call her`

**When it does NOT apply** — For advice use `should`; for permission and ability use `can`. Test: if the meaning is 'it is not necessary', use `don't have to`; if it is 'it is forbidden', use `mustn't`.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using `mustn't` for 'not necessary', because the negative of `have to` is not learned
- Adding `to` after `must` (`must to go`), or using `do` with `must`
- Writing `haves to` or `have to` after `he/she`
- Using `must` for the past

**Register and usage** — `have to` is the common spoken form; `must` is typical for signs, rules and formal instructions.

rules.title: Verb plus -ing form
rules.description:
**The idea** — Some English verbs are followed by another verb in the `-ing` form (the gerund), and not by `to` + verb. The first verb decides the pattern, so these combinations are learned in groups. The same form is used after prepositions.

**The form**
- Verb + `-ing`: `enjoy doing`, `finish working`, `avoid driving`
- Verbs of liking and dislike: `enjoy`, `mind`, `can't stand`, `don't mind`
- Verbs of ending and continuing: `finish`, `stop`, `keep`, `give up`, `carry on`
- Verbs of avoiding and suggesting: `avoid`, `suggest`, `practise`, `consider`, `imagine`
- After every preposition: `interested in learning`, `thinking about changing`, `look forward to seeing`
- The negative puts `not` before the `-ing` form: `not going`; the `-ing` form can also be the subject: `swimming is fun`

**When it applies**
- After the verbs above: signal words `enjoy`, `finish`, `avoid`, `suggest`, `mind`
- After a preposition, including `to` in `look forward to` and `be used to`
- As a noun-like subject: `reading helps`

**When it does NOT apply** — After verbs such as `want`, `decide`, `hope`, `need`, `plan`, `learn` use `to` + base verb; after modals use the bare verb. Test: if the first verb is on the `enjoy/finish/avoid/suggest` list or the word before is a preposition, use `-ing`; if it is `want/decide/hope`, use `to`.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using `to` + verb after the `-ing` group (`enjoy to cook`), because many verbs take `to`
- Using the base form after a preposition (`interested in learn`)
- Treating `to` in `look forward to` as an infinitive marker
- Confusing `stop doing` (end an action) with `stop to do` (pause in order to do)

**Register and usage** — This pattern is neutral and frequent in all registers.

rules.title: The past continuous
rules.description:
**The idea** — The past continuous shows an action that was in progress at a moment in the past. It sets the scene, and it often describes a long action that another, shorter action interrupted.

**The form**
- Positive: `was/were` + verb + `-ing`: `I was working`, `they were working`
- `was` with `I`, `he`, `she`, `it`; `were` with `you`, `we`, `they`
- Negative: `was not` (`wasn't`), `were not` (`weren't`) + `-ing`
- Question: `Was/Were` + subject + `-ing`: `What were you doing?`
- No `did` in this tense; the `-ing` spelling follows the same rules as the present continuous
- Linking words: `while`, `when`, `as` + the past continuous or the past simple

**When it applies**
- An action in progress at a stated time: signal words `at 8 o'clock`, `all evening`, `at that moment`
- A long action interrupted by a short one: `was walking when it started`
- Two actions going on at the same time: `while`
- Background description in stories

**When it does NOT apply** — For a completed action or one event after another, use the past simple. Test: if the action was already going on when something else happened, use the continuous for the long action and the simple for the short one.

**Typical mistakes**
- Leaving out the `-ing` form (`was watch`), or leaving out `was/were`
- Mixing `was` and `were` (`they was`, `he were`)
- Using the past simple for a background action in progress
- Using `did` with the past continuous (`didn't be waiting`)

**Register and usage** — It is common in storytelling, in spoken and written narrative.

rules.title: Defining relative clauses
rules.description:
**The idea** — A defining relative clause tells the listener which person or thing you mean. Without it the noun would be unclear. The clause comes right after the noun and starts with a relative pronoun.

**The form**
- People: `who` or `that`: `the woman who works here`
- Things and animals: `which` or `that`: `the book which I read`
- Possession: `whose` + noun: `the man whose car was stolen`
- Places: `where`; times: `when`; reasons: `why`
- No commas around the clause
- The pronoun replaces the noun, so do not repeat it: no `she`, `it`, `them` after it
- The pronoun can be left out when it is the object: `the book I read`, `the man you met`; never when it is the subject
- The verb agrees with the noun before the pronoun

**When it applies**
- Identifying a noun: signal words `the one who`, `the thing that`, `a person who`
- Definitions: `a mechanic is a person who ...`
- Choosing between similar things

**When it does NOT apply** — If the clause only adds extra information and is set off by commas, use a non-defining clause, where `that` is not possible. Test: if you can delete the clause and the noun is still clear, it is non-defining; if you cannot, it is defining.

**Typical mistakes**
- Repeating the noun with a pronoun (`the car that I bought it`), because the sentence is built like a main clause
- Using `which` for people and `who` for things
- Using `what` as a relative pronoun (`the book what`)
- Adding commas that make the clause non-defining
- Singular verb after a plural antecedent

**Register and usage** — `that` is neutral; `who` and `which` are slightly more formal.

rules.title: The simple passive
rules.description:
**The idea** — In the passive the subject of the sentence is the person or thing that receives the action. English uses it when the doer is unknown, unimportant or obvious, or when you want to begin with the thing affected.

**The form**
- Present passive: `am/is/are` + past participle: `is made`, `are sold`
- Past passive: `was/were` + past participle: `was built`, `were taken`
- Negative: `is not`, `was not` + participle; question: `Is it made ...?`, `Where were they taken?`
- The doer, if mentioned, comes after `by`: `by the police`
- The participle is the third form of the verb: regular `-ed`, irregular `stolen`, `written`
- `be` agrees with the new subject, not with the doer

**When it applies**
- The doer is unknown or unimportant: signal words `was stolen`, `is made`, `are spoken`
- Processes, facts and news: `is produced in`, `was founded in`
- Formal and written texts, signs, instructions

**When it does NOT apply** — If the doer is the important subject, use the active form; intransitive verbs (`arrive`, `happen`) have no passive. Test: if the sentence needs an object that becomes the subject, the passive is possible; if there is no object, it is not.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using the base form or the active form after `be` (`was break`), instead of the participle
- Using the wrong `be` (`the letters was sent`) because the doer or the last noun is used for agreement
- Using `did` for a negative passive (`didn't made`)
- Mixing up `by` with other prepositions

**Register and usage** — The passive is common in news, science and formal writing and less so in casual speech.

rules.title: Reported statements and backshift
rules.description:
**The idea** — When you report what someone said, you tell it from a later point in time. Because of this shift, the verb usually moves one step back into the past, and pronouns and time words change to fit the new speaker.

**The form**
- Reporting verb + (`that`) + clause: `she said that ...`, `he told me that ...`
- `say` has no object; `tell` needs a person: `said`, but `told me`, `told him`
- Backshift: present simple becomes past simple; present continuous becomes past continuous; present perfect and past simple become past perfect
- Modals: `will` becomes `would`, `can` becomes `could`, `may` becomes `might`; `must` often becomes `had to`
- Pronouns follow the new speaker; time words shift: `today` becomes `that day`, `tomorrow` becomes `the next day`, `now` becomes `then`
- Word order stays that of a statement; there are no quotation marks

**When it applies**
- Reporting past speech or thought: signal words `said`, `told`, `explained`, `mentioned`
- News, messages and retelling of conversations

**When it does NOT apply** — If the reporting is in the present (`she says`) or the fact is still true and just said, the tense can stay unchanged. Test: if the reporting verb is past, move the tense back; if it is present, keep it.

**Typical mistakes**
- Keeping the original present tense after `said`, because the fact feels current
- Using `said me` or `told that` without the person; `tell` needs an object and `say` does not
- Forgetting to change pronouns and time words
- Changing the tense only in one verb of a long report

**Register and usage** — In casual speech people often keep the original tense for fresh news; careful writing shifts it.
rules.llmDescription: Reported statements with said and told: say/tell confusion, missing backshift of present to past and will to would, unchanged pronouns or time words, missing object after tell.

rules.title: The second conditional
rules.description:
**The idea** — The second conditional speaks about situations that are unreal, imaginary or very unlikely now. The speaker pictures a different world and says what would happen in it. The past form signals distance from reality, not past time.

**The form**
- `if` + past simple, `would` + base verb: `if I had`, `I would buy`
- With `be`, `were` is used for all persons in careful English: `if I were you`; `was` is common in speech
- Negative: `wouldn't` + base verb; `if` + `didn't` + base verb
- Question: `What would you do if you ...?`; `Would you ... if ...?`
- Other results: `could` or `might` instead of `would`
- Never use `would` in the `if` clause (`if I would have`)

**When it applies**
- Imaginary present or future situations: signal words `if I were`, `imagine`, `suppose`
- Giving advice: `if I were you`
- Unlikely future events: `if I won the lottery`

**When it does NOT apply** — For a real, possible future use the first conditional (`if` + present, `will`); for an imaginary past use the third conditional (`if` + past perfect). Test: if the situation is unreal or unlikely now or in the future, use the past after `if` and `would` in the result.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using `would` in the `if` clause, because the result clause has it
- Using the present simple after `if`, which makes the situation real
- Using `will` in the result
- Using `is/was` instead of `were` in formal advice such as `if I were you`

**Register and usage** — `if I were you` is the fixed advice formula; both `was` and `were` occur in speech.
rules.llmDescription: Second conditional if plus past simple with would in the result for unreal present or future situations: would in the if clause, present after if, will in the result, was/were with I in advice.

rules.title: The third conditional
rules.description:
**The idea** — The third conditional looks back at the past and imagines a different result. The speaker talks about something that did not happen and what would have followed. It is the form of regret, criticism and relief.

**The form**
- `if` + past perfect, `would have` + past participle: `if I had known`, `I would have told`
- Contracted: `I'd have`, `hadn't`, `wouldn't have`
- Negative: `hadn't` + participle in the `if` part; `wouldn't have` + participle in the result
- Question: `What would you have done if ...?`
- Other results: `could have`, `might have` + participle
- Never use `would have` in the `if` clause (`if you would have asked`)

**When it applies**
- Unreal past situations: signal words `if only`, `I wish`, `too late`, `at that time`
- Regrets and criticism of past choices
- Explaining what a different event would have changed

**When it does NOT apply** — For an unreal present use the second conditional; for a possible future use the first. Test: if you look back at something that did not happen and can no longer change, use the past perfect after `if` and `would have` in the result.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using `would have` in both clauses, because the result form is copied into the `if` clause
- Using the simple past after `if`, which sounds like the second conditional
- Using the base form or past form instead of the participle in the result (`would told`, `would have went`)
- Using `will have` in the result

**Register and usage** — In speech `'d` stands for both `had` and `would`; this is common and normal.

rules.title: Present perfect continuous
rules.description:
**The idea** — The present perfect continuous looks at an activity that started in the past and is still going on, or has just stopped with a visible result. It stresses the activity and its duration, not the finished result.

**The form**
- `have/has` + `been` + verb + `-ing`: `have been working`, `has been raining`
- Negative: `haven't/hasn't been` + `-ing`
- Question: `Have/Has` + subject + `been` + `-ing`; `How long have you been ...-ing?`
- Time with `for` (length) and `since` (start); `all day`, `lately`, `recently`
- Contracted: `I've been`, `she's been`
- State verbs (`know`, `like`, `have` for possession) do not take this form; use the simple perfect

**When it applies**
- An activity that began earlier and is still happening: signal words `for`, `since`, `how long`
- A recent activity with a present result: `I'm tired because I've been running`
- Repeated actions over a period: `lately`, `recently`, `all week`

**When it does NOT apply** — If you stress a completed result or a number (`I have written three emails`), use the present perfect simple; for state verbs use the simple perfect too. Test: if the focus is on how long or on the activity, use the continuous; if it is on how much or on the result, use the simple.

**Typical mistakes**
- Dropping `been` or `-ing` (`have been wait`, `has raining`)
- Using the present continuous with `since` or `for` (`is working since 2019`), because the action is happening now
- Putting the subject in the wrong place in `how long` questions
- Using the continuous with state verbs (`have been knowing`)

**Register and usage** — It is frequent in speech to explain tiredness, delay or change.

rules.title: The past perfect
rules.description:
**The idea** — The past perfect marks an event that happened before another event in the past. It is the 'past in the past': the speaker is already telling about the past and needs to show which event came first.

**The form**
- `had` + past participle: `had finished`, `had gone`, `had seen`
- `had` is the same for all persons; contracted `I'd`, `she'd`
- Negative: `had not` (`hadn't`) + participle
- Question: `Had` + subject + participle: `Had you eaten?`
- Often with `already`, `just`, `never`, `before`, `by the time`, `after`, `until`
- Both events are usually in one sentence: past perfect for the earlier one, past simple for the later

**When it applies**
- Earlier of two past events: signal words `before`, `after`, `by the time`, `when`, `already`
- Reported speech about earlier events: `he said he had seen`
- Explaining a past situation by an earlier cause
- Third conditional (`if I had known`)

**When it does NOT apply** — If the events follow each other in order and the order is clear, use the past simple for both. Test: if you need to show that one past event was completed before another, use the past perfect for the first; if you only list events in order, use the past simple.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using the past simple for the earlier event, so the order is unclear
- Using the past perfect for both events
- Using `did` or `have` instead of `had` (`didn't have eaten`)
- Using the past form instead of the participle (`had went`)
- Placing `already` after the participle in the wrong position

**Register and usage** — It is typical of written narrative and of reports of earlier events.
rules.llmDescription: Past perfect had plus past participle for an event before another past event: past simple instead for the earlier event, wrong had forms, had went, wrong order of events, present perfect instead after reporting verb.

rules.title: The future perfect
rules.description:
**The idea** — The future perfect looks back from a point in the future and says that something will already be complete by then. The speaker stands in the future and sees an action behind them.

**The form**
- `will have` + past participle: `will have finished`, `will have gone`
- Contracted: `I'll have`, `she'll have`; negative: `won't have` + participle
- Question: `Will` + subject + `have` + participle: `Will you have finished?`
- Same form for all persons; no `-s`
- Time markers: `by` + time, `by the time`, `before`, `in two years`
- After `by the time` the verb is in the present simple, not `will`: `by the time you arrive`

**When it applies**
- A deadline for completion: signal words `by Friday`, `by then`, `by the end of the year`
- A prediction about completed events: `by 2030 they will have built`
- Guessing about something already done: `they will have arrived by now`

**When it does NOT apply** — For an action that will simply happen at a future time, use `will` or `going to`; for an action in progress at that time, use the future continuous. Test: if the key idea is 'already finished by then', use the future perfect; if it is 'will happen then', use `will`.

**Typical mistakes**
- Leaving out `have` (`will finished`), or using `has/had` instead
- Using the base form or the past form after `have` (`will have finish`)
- Using `will` after `by the time` (`by the time you will arrive`)
- Wrong question order: `How much will have you saved`
- Using the future simple where the completion by a deadline matters

**Register and usage** — It is common in planning, business and formal speech about deadlines.

rules.title: Modal verbs of deduction
rules.description:
**The idea** — English speakers show how sure they are about something with modal verbs. When they use evidence to guess, the choice of modal tells the listener how strong the conclusion is. The form also shows whether the guess is about now or about the past.

**The form**
- Present certainty: `must` + base verb (almost sure it is true)
- Present impossibility: `can't` + base verb (almost sure it is not true)
- Present possibility: `may`, `might`, `could` + base verb
- Past: modal + `have` + past participle: `must have left`, `can't have known`, `might have been`
- Continuous: modal + `be` + `-ing` (now) or `have been` + `-ing` (past)
- The opposite of `must` is `can't`, not `mustn't`; `mightn't` and `may not` mean it is possibly not true

**When it applies**
- Conclusions from evidence: signal words `probably`, `obviously`, `it seems`, `look at`
- Guessing about people, reasons and past events
- Hedging: `might`, `could`, `may` for weaker possibility

**When it does NOT apply** — For obligation or prohibition use `must/mustn't` in their rule sense; for ability use `can`. Test: if you are guessing from evidence, use `must/can't/might`; if you give a rule or a duty, use the obligation meaning.

**Typical mistakes**
- Adding `to` after the modal or using `-s` (`must to be`, `might is`)
- Using the base form for past deductions (`must rained`) instead of `have` + participle
- Using `mustn't` or `can be not` for 'impossible'
- Using `can` for possible guesses where `might` is expected
- Writing `should of` or `must of` for `have`

**Register and usage** — `must have` and `might have` are common in everyday speech.
rules.llmDescription: Deduction with must, can't, might, may, could plus base verb or have plus participle: to after modal, missing have for past deduction, mustn't or can be not for impossibility, wrong participle.

rules.title: Non-defining relative clauses
rules.description:
**The idea** — A non-defining relative clause adds extra information about a noun that is already clear. The noun does not need the clause to be understood, so the clause is separated from the rest of the sentence by commas, like a short aside.

**The form**
- Noun + comma + `who/which/whose/where/when` + clause + comma
- People: `who` or `whom`; things: `which`; possession: `whose`; places: `where`
- `that` is never used: only `who` and `which`
- The pronoun cannot be left out, even as an object
- `which` can refer to a whole idea before it: `he failed, which surprised us`
- With a preposition (formal): `in which`, `to whom`

**When it applies**
- Extra facts about names and unique things: signal words `Paris`, `my mother`, `the Nile`, `my laptop`
- Describing a noun that is already identified by a possessive, name or `this/that`
- Adding comments about a whole situation with `which`

**When it does NOT apply** — If the clause is needed to know which person or thing is meant, use a defining clause with no commas and possibly `that`. Test: if you can remove the clause and the noun is still clear, use commas and `who/which`; if not, no commas.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using `that` after a comma, because `that` is common in defining clauses
- Leaving out the commas, which makes the clause look defining
- Repeating the noun with a pronoun (`which it is old`, `which I read it`)
- Using `who's` for `whose`
- Using `who` or `whom` after `which`-type nouns, mixing people and things

**Register and usage** — Mostly written and formal; in speech the commas are heard as pauses.
rules.llmDescription: Non-defining relative clauses with commas and who, which, whose, where: that used after a comma, missing commas, repeated pronoun, who's for whose, wrong relative word for a whole clause.

rules.title: Passive with modal verbs
rules.description:
**The idea** — When a modal verb (what is possible, necessary, allowed or advisable) is combined with a passive, English builds the passive after the modal. The modal stays first, and `be` carries the passive structure.

**The form**
- Present and future: modal + `be` + past participle: `must be finished`, `can be solved`, `will be served`
- Past: modal + `have been` + past participle: `could have been repaired`, `should have been told`
- Negative: `not` after the modal: `can't be done`, `shouldn't have been sent`
- Question: modal before the subject: `Can the form be filled in?`
- With `have to`, `ought to`, `need to`, `be going to`: `has to be done`, `ought to be sent`
- The modal never changes form; only the participle changes with the verb

**When it applies**
- Rules, duties and instructions: signal words `must be`, `has to be`, `should be`
- Possibility and ability: `can be seen`, `might be lost`
- Offers, promises and plans: `will be sent`, `is going to be built`
- Regret about past events: `should have been told`

**When it does NOT apply** — If the doer is the subject, use an active modal (`you must finish it`). Test: if the thing receives the action and the doer is unknown or unimportant, put `be` + participle after the modal.

**Typical mistakes**
- Leaving out `be` (`must finished`), because the modal and participle seem enough
- Using the base verb or `-ing` instead of the participle (`can't be solve`, `has to be cleaning`)
- Writing `been` for the present or `be` for the past (`might been sold`)
- Putting `be` before the modal in questions

**Register and usage** — Common in instructions, reports and signs; it sounds impersonal and formal.
rules.llmDescription: Passive after modals: modal plus be plus past participle, and modal plus have been plus participle for the past; missing be, base or -ing instead of participle, been for be, wrong question order.

rules.title: Reported questions
rules.description:
**The idea** — When you report a question, it stops being a question and becomes part of a statement. The helper verb and the inverted order of the direct question disappear, and the clause goes back to statement word order.

**The form**
- Reporting verb + question word or `if/whether` + subject + verb: `asked where I lived`
- Wh-questions keep the question word: `where`, `what`, `why`, `when`, `how much`
- Yes/no questions use `if` or `whether`: `asked if I was hungry`
- Statement order: subject before the verb; no `do/does/did`, no inversion
- Tenses shift back as in reported statements: present becomes past, `will` becomes `would`, `can` becomes `could`
- No question mark; pronouns and time words change to fit the new speaker

**When it applies**
- After `asked`, `wondered`, `wanted to know`, `enquired`
- In polite indirect questions: signal words `could you tell me`, `do you know`
- In reports of interviews, tests and conversations

**When it does NOT apply** — For the direct question use the question order with a helper verb; for a reported statement use `that`. Test: if the clause is inside another sentence, use statement order without `do/did`; if it stands alone, use question order.

**Typical mistakes**
- Keeping the question order (`asked where did I live`), because the idea is still a question
- Keeping `do/does/did` in the reported clause
- Using `that` instead of `if/whether` for yes/no questions
- Forgetting backshift
- Adding a question mark at the end

**Register and usage** — The same order is used for indirect polite questions in present time.
rules.llmDescription: Reported and indirect questions with statement word order: inverted order or do/did kept after asked, that instead of if or whether, missing backshift, question word order in a subordinate clause.

rules.title: Inversion after negative adverbials
rules.description:
**The idea** — When a negative or restrictive adverbial opens the sentence for emphasis, English reverses subject and auxiliary verb, as in a question. The inversion gives the sentence a formal, dramatic tone.

**The form**
- Negative adverbial + auxiliary + subject + main verb: `never have I seen`
- Adverbials: `never`, `rarely`, `seldom`, `hardly ... when`, `no sooner ... than`, `not only ... but also`, `little`, `under no circumstances`, `at no time`, `only after/when/if`
- If there is no auxiliary, add `do/does/did`: `rarely do we eat`, `little did they know`
- With `be`, invert directly: `not only was he late`
- The main verb after the auxiliary is the base form or participle, never inflected twice
- The second clause after `not only` and `hardly` keeps normal order
- `hardly/scarcely` + `had` ... `when`; `no sooner` + `had` ... `than`

**When it applies**
- Emphasis in formal writing and speeches: signal words `never`, `rarely`, `only then`, `under no circumstances`
- Strong surprise or warnings

**When it does NOT apply** — If the adverbial is not at the start, use normal order. Test: if the negative word opens the sentence for emphasis, invert the subject and the auxiliary; if it stays inside the clause, do not.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using normal order after the fronted adverbial (`never I have seen`), because the adverbial is treated like a simple opener
- Inverting without an auxiliary, or adding `do` where there is already another auxiliary
- Using the wrong tense pair in `no sooner` and `hardly`
- Inverting in the second half of `not only ... but`

**Register and usage** — Formal, literary or rhetorical; rare in casual speech.
rules.llmDescription: Inversion after fronted negative adverbials never, rarely, seldom, hardly, no sooner, not only, little, under no circumstances, only after: normal subject-verb order, missing do/did, inflected verb after the auxiliary.

rules.title: Mixed conditionals
rules.description:
**The idea** — Sometimes the condition and the result belong to different times. A mixed conditional links a past condition with a present result, or a present state with a past result. The tense of each clause follows its own time.

**The form**
- Past condition, present result: `if` + past perfect, `would` + base verb: `if I had studied, I would be`
- Present or permanent condition, past result: `if` + past simple, `would have` + participle: `if I were taller, I would have played`
- Negative: `hadn't` in the `if` part; `wouldn't` + base or `wouldn't have` + participle in the result
- Other modals in the result: `could`, `might`
- Time words show the mix: `now`, `today`, `still`, `by now` with the present result; `then`, `at that time` with the past result
- Never put `would` or `would have` in the `if` clause

**When it applies**
- A past event that still affects the present: signal words `now`, `today`, `still`, `by now`
- A permanent quality that would have changed the past: `if I were`, `if I weren't so`
- Regret and explanation

**When it does NOT apply** — If both parts are in the past, use the third conditional; if both are present or future, use the second. Test: ask 'when is the condition?' and 'when is the result?'; match each verb to its own time.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using the same tense pattern in both clauses (`would have been a doctor now`), because the full third conditional is learned as one block
- Using `would` in the `if` clause
- Using `will` in the result
- Missing the participle after `would have`

**Register and usage** — Natural in discussion and reflection; neutral in tone.

rules.title: Wish and if only
rules.description:
**The idea** — `Wish` and `if only` express regret or a desire for something to be different from how it is. As in unreal conditionals, the verb moves one step back in time: the tense shows that the situation is not real, not that it is past.

**The form**
- Present situation: `wish` + past simple: `I wish I had`, `she wishes she were`
- Past situation: `wish` + past perfect: `I wish I had known`, `if only I had listened`
- Annoyance or wanting change: `wish` + `would` + base verb: `I wish you would stop`
- Ability: `wish` + `could` + base verb; `if only` is stronger and more emotional
- `were` is used for all persons in careful English; `was` is common in speech
- `wish` itself is in the present; it does not change

**When it applies**
- Regret about now or the past: signal words `I wish`, `if only`, `too late`
- Complaints about other people's behaviour: `would`
- Desires that are impossible or unlikely

**When it does NOT apply** — For a real hope about the future use `hope` + present or `will`. Test: if the wish is about something unreal, use `wish` + past form; if it is a real possibility, use `hope`.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using the present form after `wish` (`I wish I have`), because the wish concerns the present
- Using `would` for oneself or for states (`I wish I would be taller`); `would` expresses annoyance about other people
- Using the past simple for a past regret
- Using `will` or `can` after `wish`
- Mixing up `wish` and `hope`

**Register and usage** — Natural in conversation and writing; `if only` is more emphatic.
rules.llmDescription: Wishes and regrets with wish and if only: present tense after wish, would for own states, simple past for a past regret, will or can after wish, hope confused with wish.

rules.title: The mandative subjunctive
rules.description:
**The idea** — After verbs and adjectives that express a demand, suggestion, recommendation or necessity, formal English uses the bare base form of the verb in the that-clause. The clause names something that should happen, not something that happens, so the verb does not carry person, number or tense.

**The form**
- `that` + subject + base verb: `suggested that he take`, `insist that she be`
- The same form for all persons: no `-s`, no `-ed`, no `will`
- Negative: `not` before the verb, with no `do`: `that he not accept`
- Passive: `be` + participle: `that the fee be paid`
- Triggers: `suggest`, `recommend`, `demand`, `insist`, `require`, `propose`, `request`, `ask`
- Adjectives and nouns: `essential`, `vital`, `important`, `necessary`, `it is vital that`, `the requirement that`
- `that` can be omitted after verbs

**When it applies**
- Formal advice, rules and decisions: signal words `recommend that`, `insist that`, `essential that`
- Meetings, contracts, regulations and academic writing

**When it does NOT apply** — British informal English often uses `should` + base verb or the ordinary indicative instead. Test: if the that-clause states a required or recommended action, the bare verb form is available; if it reports a fact, use a normal tense.

**Typical mistakes**
- Adding `-s` after `he/she` (`that he takes`), because normal agreement is applied
- Using `is/was` instead of `be` (`that she is present`)
- Using `don't/doesn't` for the negative instead of bare `not`
- Using `will` or `would` inside the clause

**Register and usage** — Formal and written; `should` + base verb is the British alternative, and both are correct.
rules.llmDescription: Mandative subjunctive: bare base verb in that-clauses after suggest, recommend, insist, demand, require, essential, vital; -s, is/was or do-negation used instead of the bare form.

rules.title: Cleft sentences with it
rules.description:
**The idea** — A cleft sentence splits one idea into two clauses so that one part gets strong emphasis. The `it is ... that` frame places the focus word or phrase between `it is/was` and a relative-like clause, to correct, contrast or highlight.

**The form**
- `it` + `is/was` + focus + `that/who` + clause: `it was Anna who called`
- Focus can be a subject, an object, an adverbial of time, place or reason, or a phrase
- Use `who` or `that` for people, `that` for things and for adverbials; `what` is never used
- The verb after `who/that` agrees with the focus when the focus is the subject
- `be` agrees with tense, not with the focus; the singular `it was` stays even before plural nouns
- Negative focus: `it wasn't the price that bothered me`
- Question: `Was it you who ...?`

**When it applies**
- Correcting a wrong idea: signal words `it was ... not ...`, `it is because of`
- Stressing time, place or cause: `it was in Paris that`, `it was not until midnight that`
- Highlighting a person or object in writing

**When it does NOT apply** — To emphasise a whole action or a thing as a description, use the pseudo-cleft with `what` (`what I need is`). Test: if you highlight one named element from a clause, use `it is ... that`; if you highlight the whole clause with `what`, use the pseudo-cleft.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using `what`, `which` or `when` instead of `that` or `who` (`it was Anna what`)
- Using the wrong word order after `that` (`that were we married`); the clause keeps statement order
- Making `be` plural with a plural focus
- Dropping `that` after `not until`

**Register and usage** — Common in formal writing and careful speech.

rules.title: Passive reporting structures
rules.description:
**The idea** — To report what people believe, say or expect without naming who, English uses impersonal passive structures. They are typical of news, science and formal writing, where the source of the claim is general or unknown.

**The form**
- `It` + passive reporting verb + `that` clause: `it is said that`, `it was believed that`, `it is thought that`
- Personal pattern: subject + passive reporting verb + `to` + infinitive: `he is said to be`
- Earlier events: `to have` + participle: `is believed to have left`
- Continuing events: `to be` + `-ing`: `is understood to be living`
- Passive reporting verbs: `say`, `believe`, `think`, `know`, `expect`, `report`, `claim`, `allege`, `understand`, `consider`
- The `it` pattern keeps a full clause; the personal pattern has no `that`
- The personal pattern cannot be mixed with `that`: not `she is said that`

**When it applies**
- Reports in news and formal texts: signal words `is said`, `is reported`, `is believed`, `is known`
- Statements about general opinion, rumours or findings
- Hedging claims in academic writing

**When it does NOT apply** — To name the source use an active sentence (`experts believe`). Test: if the speaker is unknown or general, use `it is said that ...` or `X is said to ...`; if the speaker matters, use the active.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using a finite verb after `to` or leaving out `to` (`is said being`, `alleged have taken`)
- Using the present infinitive for earlier events instead of `to have` + participle
- Mixing both patterns (`She is said that she speaks`)
- Keeping `it` before an infinitive (`it is believed him to be`)

**Register and usage** — Mostly formal and written, in journalism, law and science.

rules.title: Participle clauses
rules.description:
**The idea** — A participle clause replaces a longer clause with a verb form that has no subject of its own. The subject is understood from the main clause. This makes writing shorter and more fluent, and it links ideas of time, reason or result.

**The form**
- Present participle (`-ing`): active meaning, same time: `walking down the street`
- Past participle (`-ed`, third form): passive meaning: `seen from the hill`, `written in a hurry`
- Perfect participle: `having` + participle: earlier action, active; `having been` + participle: earlier action, passive
- Negative: `not` before the participle: `not knowing`, `not having eaten`
- After conjunctions: `while waiting`, `before leaving`, `after finishing`
- Reduced relative clauses: `the man standing there`, `the letters written last week`
- The subject of the participle must be the same as the subject of the main clause

**When it applies**
- Two actions at the same time or one after the other: signal words `while`, `after`, `having`
- Reasons and conditions: `being tired`, `not knowing`
- Describing nouns: `the people waiting`, `the book written by`

**When it does NOT apply** — If the two clauses have different subjects, use a full clause. Test: if both actions belong to the same person or thing, a participle clause is possible; if not, keep the full clause with its own subject.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using `-ing` where the meaning is passive (`seeing from the hill` for `seen`)
- Using a base form or a finite verb instead of a participle (`having finish`, `she dropping`)
- Adding a conjunction such as `so` after the participle clause
- Using `having` + participle for a simultaneous action
- Dangling participles: the subject of the main clause does not match

**Register and usage** — Frequent in written and formal English; less natural in casual speech.
rules.llmDescription: Participle clauses with -ing, past participle and having plus participle replacing full clauses: -ing for passive meaning, base form or finite verb after the participle, extra conjunction, mismatched subject, wrong perfect participle.

rules.title: Should have and ought to have
rules.description:
**The idea** — To criticise a past action, express regret or say that something was the right thing to do but did not happen, English uses `should have` or `ought to have` with a past participle. It looks back at a past that cannot be changed.

**The form**
- `should have` + past participle: `should have gone`, `should have told`
- `ought to have` + past participle: `ought to have called`
- Negative: `shouldn't have` / `ought not to have` + participle: it was a mistake to do it
- Question: `Should I have ...?`; `Shouldn't you have ...?`
- Contracted: `should've`, `shouldn't have`; written `should have`, never `should of`
- The same form for all persons; the participle is the third form of the verb
- `be`: `should have been`

**When it applies**
- Regret about your own past: signal words `I wish`, `too late`, `if only`
- Criticism of others: `you should have asked`
- Describing the right action that did not take place
- Expectation that something has already happened: `they should have arrived by now`

**When it does NOT apply** — For advice about the present or future use `should` + base verb; for a deduction use `must have`. Test: if the action is already over and was not done, or was done wrongly, use `should have` + participle; if you give advice for now, use `should` + base.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using the past simple or the base form after `should` (`should went`, `should tell`), because `have` is dropped
- Writing `should of` or `shouldn't of`, from the way `'ve` sounds
- Using the wrong participle (`should have took`, `should have being`)
- Using `ought` without `to`

**Register and usage** — `should have` is neutral; `ought to have` is more formal and less common.

rules.title: Preposition before whom and which
rules.description:
**The idea** — In formal English a preposition can move to the front of a relative clause, before the relative pronoun. The pronoun is then in an object form, and the clause sounds careful and written.

**The form**
- Preposition + `whom` for people: `the person to whom I spoke`, `the colleagues with whom I work`
- Preposition + `which` for things: `the house in which we lived`, `the method by which`
- `who` and `that` cannot follow a preposition
- Informal alternative: preposition at the end: `the person I spoke to`, `the house we lived in`
- Quantifiers: `most of whom`, `some of which`, `none of whom`
- The relative pronoun cannot be left out when the preposition comes first
- Possession: `whose` stays the same

**When it applies**
- Formal writing, speeches and legal texts: signal words `the person to whom`, `in which`, `by which`
- Non-defining clauses with quantifiers: `many of whom`
- Choosing precision over a natural spoken order

**When it does NOT apply** — In speech and informal writing the preposition normally stays at the end, with `who`, `that` or no pronoun. Test: if the preposition comes before the pronoun, use `whom` or `which`; if it stays at the end, use `who`, `that` or nothing.

**Typical mistakes**
- Using `who` or `that` after a preposition (`to who`, `in that`), because they are the usual relative pronouns
- Using `what` instead of `which` (`for what`)
- Repeating the preposition at the end as well
- Using `whom` without a preposition in informal contexts and adding a second pronoun

**Register and usage** — Formal and written; sounds stiff in casual conversation.
rules.llmDescription: Formal relative clauses with a preposition before whom or which, including quantifiers most of whom and some of which: who, that or what used after a preposition, repeated preposition.
